title: Hyperscaler-adjacent customers, Nvidia-aligned supply
body:
## Who Was Buying — and Why That Mattered

Nebius did not publish a customer list. That was not an oversight. It was characteristic of the segment it had chosen to serve.

The enterprise AI infrastructure market operates through multi-year framework agreements signed under non-disclosure, a contracting culture imported from the hyperscalers whose overflow Nebius was explicitly designed to absorb. The company described its customer base in structural terms rather than by name: AI laboratories and foundation-model developers consuming GPU compute for training runs; multi-cloud enterprise buyers who required burst capacity outside a primary hyperscaler relationship; and production inference customers deploying at scale and seeking guaranteed resource availability. What Nebius's disclosure did confirm — in the [February 2026 Q4 earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) — was that more than half of its $7–9 billion FY2026 annual recurring revenue target was already contracted by the time those results were published. That single data point defined the company's revenue quality in a way that customer names could not.

The distinction between contracted ARR and spot-market GPU cloud revenue was not cosmetic. Spot AI cloud markets — the GPU rental services that priced H100 access by the hour — carried structural churn risk tied to model-training cycle lengths, lab funding cycles, and capacity overhang from incumbent hyperscalers. Multi-year commercial commitments from enterprise buyers of Nebius's scale meant credit-worthy counterparties had signed binding purchase obligations, providing revenue visibility of a kind more common to enterprise software than to cloud-infrastructure businesses at an equivalent growth rate. The $834 million in operating cash flow Nebius generated in Q4 2025 alone — against $227.7 million in revenue — reflected that contracting structure directly: customer prepayments accruing well ahead of recognised revenue, a balance-sheet signature associated with hyperscaler-style commercial terms rather than spot-market rentals.

## The Nvidia Equation

No single relationship on Nebius's counterparty map carried as much strategic weight as the one with Nvidia.

In August 2025, Nebius closed a $700 million [oversubscribed strategic equity placement](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-announces-oversubscribed-strategic-equity-financing-of-usd-700-million-to-accelerate-roll-out-of-full-stack-ai-infrastructure), with Nvidia participating alongside Accel and Orbis Investments. The placement was not a passive financial investment. Nvidia's decision to take an equity stake in an AI cloud company — at a moment when it was simultaneously the dominant supplier of the compute those clouds required — created a category of alignment that constrained how to think about Nebius's GPU supply position. The company did not publicly disclose specific allocation terms or volumes. What it did make visible was the broader logic: a GPU supplier that held equity in a customer had interests that diverged sharply from a purely transactional supplier-customer relationship.

Nvidia's GPU roadmap, running through the H100 and H200 generations to the B100 and B200 Blackwell architecture and into the Rubin platform, was the backbone of every serious AI cloud business's capacity plan in 2025. The allocation question — who received priority in a supply-constrained environment — was the defining competitive variable for independent AI cloud operators. CoreWeave, the closest comparable public company at the time, had established its Nvidia relationship through years of early-adopter purchasing and had similarly positioned that alignment as a structural advantage. Nebius's $700 million placement inserted Nvidia as a financial co-owner at a moment when Nebius was simultaneously planning the most aggressive capital expenditure program any AI-cloud company had publicly committed to: $16–20 billion in capex across FY2026.

The implied logic was circular in the best sense. Nvidia's equity stake gave it a financial incentive to see Nebius's capacity ramp succeed. Nebius's capacity ramp required GPU allocations at scale. A supplier whose equity value increased with a customer's growth had structurally different behaviour than one negotiating at arm's length. None of that was guaranteed. Specific allocation commitments were not in the public record. But the geometry of the relationship was visible enough that the August 2025 placement was, in effect, a public signal from Nvidia about which independent AI cloud operators it considered strategically important.

## Power as the Binding Constraint

If GPU allocation was the most consequential uncertainty, power was the slowest-moving constraint.

Nebius exited 2025 with 170 megawatts of connected power against more than 2,000 megawatts under contract. That 12-to-1 gap between contracted and active power capacity was not a sign of idle strategy — it was a map of the construction pipeline. Power utility agreements, site acquisitions, grid interconnections, cooling infrastructure, and data centre build-out each carried their own lead times, regulatory dependencies, and execution risk. Nebius's FY2026 target of 800–1,000 megawatts of connected power represented a five- to six-fold physical expansion in a single year. The company's European footprint — centred on Finland, where the legacy Yandex data centre infrastructure provided a starting base — was being supplemented by US site development as the company pursued geographic diversification of its capacity.

The practical execution sequence was constrained by physics rather than capital. Money could accelerate site acquisition and vendor commitments. It could not compress utility interconnection timelines or the lead times on large-format cooling deployments. The $2 billion in capital expenditure Nebius deployed in Q4 2025 alone — a 9-to-1 capex-to-revenue ratio for that quarter — demonstrated the company's willingness to spend ahead of revenue. Whether the physical infrastructure could commission fast enough to meet the contracted customer obligations was the operational question that the FY2026 guidance window would answer.

The hardware supply chain sitting between GPU procurement and operational data centre capacity was not separately disclosed at the vendor level. Based on publicly available information about comparable AI infrastructure deployments, the likely server and networking vendors included Supermicro, Dell, HPE, and contract manufacturers including Foxconn-FII and direct ODM suppliers building to Nebius's specifications. These were not differentiated relationships — they were the standard supply chain for any company purchasing Nvidia GPU clusters at scale. The differentiation resided upstream, in the Nvidia relationship itself, and downstream, in the contracted customer base.

## The Investor Constellation

The three co-investors in the August 2025 placement read as a deliberate construction of the capital-structure argument.

Accel, the tier-one venture capital firm, brought enterprise software credibility and an AI-infrastructure portfolio that complemented Nebius's strategic positioning. The placement brought Accel partner Matthew Weigand onto the Nebius board — an observer seat that converted to a full board election at the August 2025 annual general meeting. Accel's presence signalled that sophisticated enterprise-technology investors had underwritten the transition from restructuring story to operating-business story.

Orbis Investments, the South African-rooted global value manager, added a different dimension. Orbis's capital profile — patient, multi-year, drawn to structural re-ratings rather than momentum — suggested the placement was attracting investors whose time horizon matched the construction cycle rather than the quarterly earnings cadence. For a company planning $16–20 billion in FY2026 capital expenditure, long-duration equity capital from a value-oriented institution carried different implications than speculative growth allocation.

Nvidia's role has been discussed above. The combination of the three produced a $700 million placement that was simultaneously a strategic validation, a supplier-alignment signal, and a capital-structure reinforcement — arriving at the precise moment when Nebius was beginning its most aggressive infrastructure ramp.

## Positioned but Not Moated

The competitive framing for Nebius at the May 2026 snapshot date required intellectual honesty about the nature of its advantages.

| Operator | Status | Balance Sheet | Nvidia Alignment | Power (Active) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nebius (NBIS) | Public, NASDAQ | $3.7B cash | Strategic equity investor | 170MW → 800-1,000MW guided |
| CoreWeave (CRWV) | Public, NASDAQ | More leveraged | Deep procurement relationship | Larger active footprint |
| Lambda | Private | VC-backed | Nvidia-aligned | Undisclosed |
| Crusoe | Private | VC-backed | Nvidia-aligned | Differentiated (flared-gas power) |
| Azure AI / GCP / AWS | Internal divisions | Balance-sheet unlimited | Preferred customer status | Multi-gigawatt at scale |

Nebius was differentiated by the cash position and by the formalised Nvidia equity alignment. Those were real advantages. They were not irreplaceable moats. CoreWeave had a larger active deployment base. The hyperscalers had unlimited capital and existing customer relationships. Lambda and Crusoe were competing for the same AI-lab customers in overlapping geographies. Vultr and DigitalOcean Nimbus addressed the smaller-scale end of the market but were not structurally comparable at the contracted-ARR level Nebius was playing at.

The structural observation that mattered was this: the case for Nebius's FY2026 revenue and ARR targets rested on three things executing concurrently — GPU allocations arriving on the cadence implied by the Nvidia relationship, power infrastructure commissioning at the rate required to support the 800–1,000 megawatt target, and the contracted customer base remaining in place and drawing against its committed obligations. Each of those was plausible on the available evidence. None was guaranteed. The FY2026 guidance window — the most aggressive capacity-build target in the public AI-cloud peer set — was simultaneously the company's strongest commercial signal and its most demanding operational test. The cash, the contracts, and the Nvidia equity stake had created the conditions for the ramp. Whether the physical infrastructure could be built fast enough to honour those conditions was the year's defining question.
